content.overview: Many plant problems share visual symptoms. The safest learning approach is to describe the pattern, check basic environment/root-zone conditions, list plausible causes and make the smallest evidence-supported correction instead of stacking products and changes.

vocabulary.definition: A proposed explanation that can be tested against observations.
A changing factor that makes it harder to identify what caused an outcome.
Returning a recent controllable change toward the prior known condition when evidence supports doing so.

sections.title: Describe before diagnosing
sections.body: Note which leaves, which plants, where in the room and how quickly the symptom changed before naming a deficiency or disease.

sections.title: Check basics before adding products
sections.body: Irrigation, root condition, pH/EC context, temperature/RH, light and pest signs can create look-alike symptoms.

sections.title: Change fewer variables
sections.body: If several inputs are changed at once, improvement or decline cannot be assigned confidently to any one action.

workedExamples: Yellowing limited to one overwatered plant is different evidence from uniform yellowing across the whole crop.
If a problem begins immediately after a major feed change, compare the prior baseline before adding another supplement.
commonMistakes: Buying a product for every symptom chart.
Making five changes in one day.
content.practicalApplication: Write the symptom, three plausible causes, the evidence for each and one low-risk test or correction. Reobserve before adding another change.
content.summary: Home troubleshooting improves when observations and controlled changes replace product stacking and guesswork.
